beginner: Prices rose 2.4% over the past year, which is close to normal and means your money isn't losing value as fast as it was before.
The economy grew very fast in the last three months, which means businesses are hiring and people have jobs.
The Federal Reserve decided not to cut interest rates this month, so borrowing money will stay expensive for a while longer.
moderate: February CPI came in at 2.4% annually with core inflation at 2.5%, showing price growth has stabilized near the Fed's 2% target after years of running hot. This is significantly better than the 8.4% peak inflation in 2022, though the Fed remains cautious about cutting rates too quickly.
Third quarter GDP expanded at 4.4% annualized, nearly double the full-year forecast of 2.2%, indicating the economy has shifted into a stronger growth phase than expected heading into 2026.

The Fed held rates steady at its March meeting while signaling only one cut may come in 2026, reflecting confidence in both growth momentum and the progress inflation has made rather than economic weakness.
expert: February CPI printed 0.3% month-over-month and 2.4% year-over-year, with core at 0.2% and 2.5% respectively, positioning inflation within striking distance of the Fed's symmetrical 2% target and reducing the urgency for rate cuts despite full-year forecasts of 2.3% average inflation.

Real GDP growth of 4.4% in Q3 2025 substantially outpaced consensus expectations and the 2.2% full-year forecast, suggesting either a structural shift in potential output or temporary cyclical strength that may not persist if external shocks (geopolitical, trade) materialize.

Vanguard's projection of a single 2026 rate cut signals the Fed will prioritize a data-dependent approach despite the strong growth backdrop, keeping the terminal rate around 3.25% and positioning monetary policy as a structural headwind to asset valuations if long-duration growth expectations remain elevated.

beginner: Canada's unemployment rate is 6.74%, which is higher than the USA's 4.4%, meaning more Canadians are out of work.
Canada is part of a group of countries working together on shipping safety in the Middle East, which could affect trade and the cost of goods.
The government keeps interest rates at 2.25%, lower than the US, to help the economy grow since it's facing some headwinds.
moderate: Unemployment stands at 6.74% in Canada, substantially above the 4.2% full-year forecast, reflecting persistent labor market weakness that has pressured the government into rate cuts while the Fed remains on hold. This divergence has widened the policy gap between the two neighbors to nearly 140 basis points.

Canada joined a major joint statement on March 19 with the UK, France, Germany, Japan and others regarding Middle East tensions and the Strait of Hormuz, raising the risk that energy price spikes or supply chain disruptions could undermine the 1.7% full-year GDP growth forecast.

February unemployment and January trade balance data arrive this week, with both critical for assessing whether the economy is stabilizing after recent labor market deterioration or whether further rate cuts will be needed.
expert: Canadian unemployment at 6.74% (vs. 6.5% full-year forecast) signals the labor market has already underperformed consensus, forcing the Bank of Canada into an easing cycle while the Fed remains on hold, creating a 140 basis point policy spread that will likely steepen the Canadian dollar's depreciation trajectory.

The Strait of Hormuz joint statement signals geopolitical risk elevation; Canada's energy export dependence and manufacturing exposure make it uniquely vulnerable to supply shock pass-through, potentially triggering stagflationary dynamics that would make further BoC cuts counterproductive if CPI re-accelerates.

February unemployment and January trade data due this week will provide early March labor and goods flow signals that could shift expectations for the April BoC meeting, particularly if the unemployment print undershoots 6.5% or trade swings back positive, validating the soft-landing narrative.

beginner: The UK's inflation is 3.18%, higher than most other big countries, which means prices are going up faster there than in America or Japan.
The UK economy is growing slowly and could slip into recession if energy prices spike from Middle East problems, so times might get tougher.
The Bank of England keeps rates at 3.75%, which is higher than Canada's but similar to the US, to keep inflation from getting worse.
moderate: The UK sits among the low-growth economies most exposed to recession risk from energy shocks, with CPI at 3.18% already above the 2.5% full-year forecast and unemployment at 5.2%, leaving little policy room to respond if geopolitical tensions push oil prices higher.

February PMI data showed the UK growing faster than the US in that month, yet full-year expectations of just 1.5% growth reflect structural headwinds from Brexit friction, labor shortages, and constrained investment that make the economy fragile relative to peers.

The UK joined the March 19 joint statement on Middle East security, underscoring that any Strait of Hormuz disruption would hit UK manufacturing and consumer energy costs hard, potentially forcing the Bank of England to choose between supporting growth and defending against inflation re-acceleration.
expert: UK CPI at 3.18% (vs. 2.5% full-year forecast) and unemployment at 5.2% (vs. 5% consensus) reflect an economy that has struggled to achieve the disinflationary trajectory seen in the US and Canada, while the 3.75% policy rate constrains room for countercyclical easing if growth rolls over.

The IMF and consensus identifiers explicitly flag the UK as a low-growth economy vulnerable to recession from energy shocks; combined with February PMI outperformance versus the US, this suggests recent strength is cyclical rather than structural, likely reversing if Brent crude breaches $100/bbl from Hormuz tensions.

The Strait of Hormuz joint statement raises the probability of a mid-year energy shock that would simultaneously push UK CPI above 3.5% and growth below 1%, forcing the BoE into a policy bind where rate cuts would risk further inflation drift while tightening would deepen recession risk in an already fragile demand environment.

beginner: Japan's unemployment rate is just 2.4%, the lowest among these four countries, which means almost everyone who wants a job can find one.
Japan's economy is expected to grow only 0.9% in 2026, much slower than the USA, so growth will be modest and wages may not rise as fast.
Japan joined other countries on March 19 in a statement about Middle East shipping, which could affect the cost of energy and goods that Japan imports.
moderate: Japan's 2.4% unemployment rate (vs. 2.5% full-year forecast) reflects a persistently tight labor market despite deflation fears, with CPI at only 1.53%, suggesting wage pressures remain intact even as growth is expected to decelerate to 0.9% in 2026 from 1.2% in 2025.

Japan's 0.75% policy rate remains well below peers, leaving room for future cuts if external demand weakens, but the recent geopolitical statement joining other leaders on Middle East security signals Japan's vulnerability to energy import shocks given its heavy reliance on crude imports.

February PMI data showed Japan growing faster than the US in that month, indicating recent strength in manufacturing despite the full-year forecast of only 0.9% expansion, suggesting near-term momentum that could fade if supply-chain disruptions or energy prices accelerate mid-year.
expert: Japan's 2.4% unemployment and 1.53% CPI readings sit within forecast ranges but highlight the unusual policy asymmetry: the BoJ holds rates at 0.75% while labor markets are tight and real rates are deeply negative, signaling commitment to sustained ultra-loose policy despite modest inflation drift upward.

The 2026 GDP forecast of 0.9% (down from 1.2%) reflects external headwinds outweighing a modest domestic recovery, and the Strait of Hormuz joint statement implies Japan faces acute energy import risk; a sustained oil shock above $100/bbl would likely push CPI above 2% while capping growth, challenging the BoJ's confidence in a virtuous wage-price spiral.

Recent February PMI outperformance relative to the US suggests Japan's manufacturing exports may be outpacing consensus expectations in early 2026, but this tailwind will reverse if Hormuz tensions crimp global goods demand, forcing the BoJ to tolerate 2% inflation while growth falls toward 0%, a stagflation scenario few in Tokyo are pricing.

beginner: Germany's economy is growing very slowly right now, and experts worry it could slip into recession if energy prices spike again.
Inflation in Germany is 2.08%, which is manageable, and unemployment sits at 3.6%, meaning most people who want jobs can find them.
Germany joined other world leaders on March 19 to discuss the situation in the Strait of Hormuz, a critical shipping route for oil and trade.
moderate: Germany is among Europe's sluggish economies and faces recession risk even from moderate energy shocks, a vulnerability that reflects its energy-intensive manufacturing base and reliance on imported fuel.
Unemployment at 3.6% remains tight despite weak growth, suggesting the labor market has not yet adjusted to slower economic conditions, though this could change if weakness persists.
The ECB holds its policy rate at 2.15%, but the geopolitical tensions around the Strait of Hormuz signal potential upside risks to energy prices that could complicate any future rate cuts.
expert: Germany's sub-trend growth trajectory exposes it to asymmetric downside risk from supply shocks in a way that higher-growth peers avoid, particularly given manufacturing's 23% share of GDP and petrochemical sector vulnerability.

The 3.6% unemployment rate masks nascent slack emerging in labor market indicators (job vacancy ratios contracting quarter-over-quarter), suggesting the Beveridge curve may be shifting even as headline jobless claims remain benign.

With CPI at 2.08% and the ECB's terminal rate guidance pointing to 2.5%, the central bank has limited room to ease if a Strait of Hormuz supply disruption forces energy prices higher and pushes demand destruction deeper into 2026.

beginner: France's economy is growing slowly at 0.7% this year, which means jobs are being created but at a modest pace.
Inflation is barely there at 0.29%, so your money goes almost as far as it did a year ago, though unemployment at 7.7% remains a concern.
France expects growth to pick up slightly to 0.9% in 2026 and 1.1% in 2027 as the economy stabilizes.
moderate: France's 0.7% growth in 2025 depends heavily on inventory rebuilding, especially in the aeronautics sector, making the economy vulnerable if companies stop restocking sooner than expected.

Deflation concerns are minimal with CPI at 0.29%, but the 7.7% unemployment rate is stubbornly high compared to Germany's 3.6%, signaling structural labor market weakness that growth alone may not fix.

The ECB holds rates at 2.15% but faces a dilemma: weak growth argues for cuts, yet the Strait of Hormuz tensions could disrupt energy supplies and reignite inflation, forcing the central bank to pause any easing cycle.
expert: France's 2025 growth profile is backward-looking, front-loaded by aeronautics inventory accumulation that peaked in Q4 2024; the forward guidance of 0.9% for 2026 assumes demand-led acceleration that has not yet materialized in consumer or investment data.

The 7.7% unemployment rate reflects both cyclical weakness and structural rigidities in the French labor market (high minimum wage indexation, employment regulation costs), creating a wage-growth ceiling that limits policy rate cuts despite subdued inflation at 0.29%.

Budget deficit forecasts of 4.8% of GDP imply fiscal support remaining elevated through 2026, but this assumes no revenue surprises; if geopolitical tensions push energy prices above 95 dollars per barrel, fiscal drag from lower VAT revenues could force austerity that deepens the growth shortfall.

beginner: Italy's economy is growing slowly like the rest of Europe, and unemployment at 5.2% is relatively low by Italian standards.
Inflation at 1.8% is mild, so prices are not rising much, and interest rates from the central bank are at 2.15%.
Italy is expected to release its latest GDP figures this week, which will show whether the economy is keeping pace with modest growth forecasts.
moderate: Italy joined the March 19 joint statement on Strait of Hormuz security, signaling alignment with other major economies on geopolitical risk, but the real story for Italy is its 5.2% unemployment rate, which remains elevated despite gradual recovery.

Inflation at 1.8% gives the ECB room to cut rates if growth weakens further, but Italy's 3.2% budget deficit forecast limits fiscal response options, making monetary policy the primary tool for supporting demand.

The upcoming GDP data release this week will clarify whether Italy is tracking toward the 1% full-year growth forecast or falling further behind, a distinction that matters for financial market pricing of ECB rate decisions in coming months.
expert: Italy's unemployment at 5.2% masks regional dispersion (southern regions above 8%) and youth joblessness (20%+), suggesting that headline growth recovery is not translating uniformly into labor market tightening or wage acceleration.

CPI at 1.8% provides the ECB with roughly 70 basis points of easing cushion before deflation risk emerges, but this assumes no Strait of Hormuz supply shock; energy price spikes would compress real incomes in an economy already facing budget consolidation headwinds.

The 3.2% budget deficit projection implies minimal fiscal space for counter-cyclical stimulus if this week's GDP print signals a downside miss; Italy's limited policy optionality means the country faces the highest recession probability in the eurozone if external demand deteriorates further.

beginner: China's economy is expected to grow 4.6% this year, which is slower than before but still solid, supported by government policies to boost spending.
Inflation is very low at 0.23%, meaning prices are barely rising, so the central bank has room to support growth if needed.
China's National People's Congress is happening now and released new inflation data, showing the government is focused on managing the economy carefully as global uncertainties persist.
moderate: China's 4.6% growth forecast sits below the 5% implied trend, but Deloitte projects 4.5% under more expansionary fiscal assumptions, suggesting consensus expects policy support to remain aggressive through 2026.

CPI at 0.23% is deeply disinflationary and gives China's central bank ample room to ease, though the policy rate sits at 2.75% (higher than the ECB's 2.15%), indicating the PBOC has maintained a more hawkish stance relative to global peers.

The National People's Congress timing coincides with fresh consumer and producer price updates, a signal that Beijing is managing expectations around deflation risks even as it pursues targeted fiscal measures to stabilize growth.
expert: China's 4.6% 2026 forecast (versus 4.7% full-year guidance) reflects consensus expectation of mild sequential deceleration, but the Deloitte 4.5% scenario hinges on fiscal multiplier assumptions that depend on credit allocation efficiency in state-owned enterprises, a variable with widening uncertainty.

The 0.23% CPI print signals core deflation pressure persisting through early 2026 despite prior stimulus; this disinflationary backdrop constrains the PBOC's ability to cut rates without triggering capital outflow concerns, creating a trilemma between growth support, currency stability, and yield differentials versus the Fed.

Budget deficit at 6.8% of GDP is the highest among the four economies analyzed, indicating China has deployed maximum fiscal headroom; if growth disappoints relative to 4.6% in coming quarters, policy levers are exhausted, forcing reliance on monetary accommodation and potential yuan depreciation to sustain external demand.

beginner: India's economy is growing fast, which means more jobs and higher incomes for ordinary people.
Prices are staying low (inflation at 1.33%), so your money buys more things than it did before.
The government is spending heavily on roads, ports, and power plants, which creates construction jobs and makes the country work better.
moderate: India's 6.6% growth forecast for 2026 significantly outpaces the broader South Asia region at 5.6%, driven by domestic consumption that remains resilient even as global trade slows.
Inflation at 1.33% in January sits well below the full-year forecast of 4.2%, giving the central bank room to cut rates if growth momentum fades, unlike peers facing price pressure.

Strong tourist arrivals from India's neighbors (127,353 from India alone to Sri Lanka) and infrastructure-led public investment create a self-reinforcing cycle where construction spending supports consumption.
expert: January CPI of 1.33% reflects a deflationary tilt that diverges sharply from the 4.2% full-year forecast, signaling either base effects from prior-year weakness or sustained demand softness that the RBI's 5.25% policy rate may be starting to accommodate.

The 6.6% growth projection for 2026 (versus the 6.3% full-year consensus) rests on public investment multipliers and household consumption elasticity that remain sensitive to credit conditions, particularly as the policy rate trajectory becomes clearer in Q2.

If inflation remains anchored below 2% through Q2, the RBI faces pressure to engineer rate cuts that could overstimulate credit growth and widen the current account deficit, currently forecast at 1.2% of GDP.

beginner: South Africa's economy will grow more slowly than most other countries, making it harder for companies to hire new workers.
Interest rates are high (6.75%), so borrowing money for a car, house, or business is expensive.
Global trade slowdowns and expensive borrowing costs are hurting businesses and keeping growth weak.
moderate: Africa's 4.0% growth projection for 2026 marks only marginal improvement from 2025's 3.9%, but South Africa itself is forecast to grow just 1.5%, making it a significant regional underperformer despite holding the continent's largest economy.

CPI at 3.49% in January sits comfortably within the SARB's 3% to 6% target band, yet the policy rate of 6.75% remains elevated, reflecting persistent wage and energy cost pressures that constrain both demand and business investment.

Global trade headwinds hit South Africa disproportionately because the country depends on commodity exports and Chinese demand, while domestic structural constraints (unemployment above 32%) limit domestic demand as an offset.
expert: January CPI of 3.49% tracks toward the upper half of the SARB's forecast band, but the 1.5% full-year GDP growth projection suggests demand-side slack is widening, creating a rare opportunity for policy normalization if inflation continues to track toward 3.5%.

The 6.75% policy rate, set in February, represents a hold despite the growth miss, signaling the SARB's concern over wage-setting dynamics and electricity costs rather than demand-driven price pressures, a structural constraint that rate cuts alone cannot resolve.

Unemployment at 32.5% (structural and forecast) indicates that even if GDP accelerates to the upside, labor market participation gains remain elusive without sectoral reallocation; tourism inflows (Russian arrivals at 59,795) offer a partial offset but cannot close the employment gap.

beginner: Brazil's central bank set interest rates at 15%, which is very high and makes borrowing expensive for people and businesses.
Inflation is running at 4.44%, close to where the government wants it, but the high interest rates are slowing job creation.
The government is considering tariffs on imported steel to protect local producers, but this could make prices go up for consumers.
moderate: Brazil's unemployment at 6.78% in February tracks below the full-year forecast of 6.5%, suggesting labor market tightness persists despite the central bank's aggressive 15.0% policy rate, which is among the highest in the world.

Inflation at 4.44% in January is already above the full-year forecast of 4.2%, and the government is considering sector-specific tariffs on steel despite heavy Chinese investment dependence, a move that risks reigniting price pressures even as rates remain restrictive.

The central bank's 15% rate, set in February, reflects both inflation fighting and currency stability concerns, but GDP data expected this week will determine whether the economy is slowing fast enough to justify eventual cuts without triggering a wage-price spiral.
expert: January CPI of 4.44% exceeds the full-year 4.2% forecast by 40 basis points, and February unemployment at 6.78% sits 28 basis points above full-year guidance, indicating that the 15.0% policy rate is extracting a real output cost without yet delivering disinflationary momentum, suggesting the Selic may have peaked.

Steel tariff threats against China despite Brazilian reliance on Chinese capital inflows create a policy inconsistency that markets may test if external financing conditions tighten, particularly given the 2.6% current account deficit forecast and the political economy of tariff reversals.

GDP data due this week carries outsized signaling value: if Q4 2025 growth was below 1% annualized, the central bank has room to begin cuts in Q2, but tariff implementation would likely force a pivot to hold or tighten, creating a policy fork that asset prices are pricing in with elevated volatility.

beginner: Russia's economy is barely growing because the war in Ukraine disrupts trade, supplies, and investment.
Prices are rising at 6.01%, higher than normal, making things more expensive for Russian families.
Interest rates are 15.5%, very high, which means Russian businesses and people pay a lot to borrow money.
moderate: CIS growth is projected at 2.1% for 2026, mostly flat from 2025, as the ongoing Ukraine conflict continues to impose direct costs (military spending, capital flight) and indirect costs (sanctions, supply disruptions) that prevent normalization.

January CPI at 6.01% sits above the 4.7% full-year forecast, and the 15.5% policy rate in February signals the central bank is still fighting inflation from excess demand and ruble depreciation, despite the economy's weak underlying growth momentum.

Russia's unemployment at 2.15% in December masks severe sectoral misallocation (military mobilization, emigration of young workers), so traditional Phillips curve relationships are broken, and any rate cuts risk rekindling inflation without stimulating productive investment.
expert: January CPI of 6.01% sits 130 basis points above the full-year 4.7% forecast, indicating that ruble depreciation and import-price pass-through remain live risks; the 15.5% policy rate set in February reflects the Bank of Russia's need to manage both demand-side wage pressures and currency stability in a capital-flight environment.

The 2.1% growth projection for 2026 is roughly half the 4% trend pre-2022, and with unemployment at 2.15% (forecast 2.5%), the economy is running at capacity in military-relevant sectors while experiencing secular decline in civilian investment and tourism (though Russian arrivals to Sri Lanka at 59,795 show some mobility).

Forward guidance: if sanctions tighten further or ruble depreciation accelerates beyond 10% year-to-date, the central bank will likely hold the 15.5% rate through 2026 rather than cut, locking in stagflation and deepening capital misallocation away from productive civilian sectors.

beginner.label: Iran Closes World's Busiest Oil Route
beginner.body: Iran shut down the Strait of Hormuz, where 20% of global oil passes. Oil prices jumped above $100 for the first time in four years. The crisis started after U.S. and Israeli attacks on Iran.

beginner.label: Stock Markets Fall Hard
beginner.body: U.S. stocks dropped sharply this week. The S&P 500 fell over 1% Friday, hitting its lowest level this year. Energy stocks rose, but most everything else fell on inflation fears.

beginner.label: Higher Oil Prices Threaten Economy
beginner.body: When oil prices stay high, it makes everything more expensive. Gas, food, and shipping costs all go up. This forces central banks to keep interest rates high instead of cutting them.

moderate.label: Iran Closes World's Busiest Oil Route
moderate.body: Iran has effectively shut the Strait of Hormuz since early March, blocking roughly 20% of global oil supplies. Brent crude surged above $100 per barrel for the first time in four years. The crisis began after joint U.S.-Israeli strikes on Iran that included killing Iran's supreme leader. Over 150 ships now sit stranded outside the strait.

moderate.label: Stock Markets Fall Hard
moderate.body: U.S. stocks suffered their fourth straight weekly decline, with the S&P 500 dropping 1.5% Friday to hit 2026 lows. The Dow fell over 400 points as bond yields jumped to 4.4%. Higher oil prices are stoking inflation fears and crushing hopes for Federal Reserve rate cuts. Only energy and financial stocks gained ground.

moderate.label: Higher Oil Prices Threaten Economy
moderate.body: The oil shock threatens to create stagflation - high inflation with slow growth. Goldman Sachs warns sustained oil prices above $100 could trigger recessions in major importing countries. Global economic growth forecasts are being cut as businesses face higher energy costs. Central banks may need to raise rates instead of cutting them to fight inflation.

expert.label: Iran Closes World's Busiest Oil Route
expert.body: Iran has effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz since March 4, disrupting 20 million barrels per day of oil flows. Brent crude hit $126 at its peak, marking the fastest oil price surge in recent conflict history. The crisis follows joint U.S.-Israeli strikes that killed Iran's supreme leader on February 28. More than 3 million barrels per day of refining capacity in the Gulf has shut down due to attacks and lack of viable export routes. Iran's IRGC warns oil could hit $200 per barrel if the blockade continues.

expert.label: Stock Markets Fall Hard
expert.body: Equity markets are pricing a 35% recession probability, up from 10% two weeks ago, according to regime models. The S&P 500 dropped 1.5% Friday, falling below its 200-day moving average for the fourth consecutive weekly decline. The Russell 2000 entered correction territory with a 2.3% drop as small caps face higher rate sensitivity. Bond yields surged to 4.4% from 3.97% pre-war as oil-driven inflation expectations crush Fed easing bets. The VIX climbed as geopolitical risk premiums expand across asset classes.

expert.label: Higher Oil Prices Threaten Economy
expert.body: The energy shock resembles the 1970s crisis in scale but with modern supply chain vulnerabilities. Goldman Sachs models show sustained Brent at $98 in Q2 would cut global GDP by 0.7% and push inflation to 5.1%. The IEA released 400 million barrels from strategic reserves, but this covers only 20 days of normal Hormuz flows. European natural gas prices doubled to over €60/MWh as LNG supplies from Qatar remain disrupted. Industrial chemical and steel manufacturers have imposed 30% surcharges, signaling broader inflationary transmission mechanisms are activating.
